A1.justification: Despite a new title and substantially different method, both PDFs concern the same CPR research and retain the ITCPR benchmark. Both documents are readable and materially complete, including v4's Appendices A–C; v3 contains no separate appendix.

before.justification: v3 reports original Word4Per retrieval results, ablations, qualitative analyses, and timing measurements in Tables I–VI and Section V.

after.justification: v4 reports original synthetic-data experiments, FAFA retrieval results, component ablations, and CIRR evaluation in Tables 1–2, Table S3, and the appendices.

M1.justification: v3's CLIP fine-tuning and TINet pseudo-word pipeline is replaced by synthetic-triplet generation and FAFA. v4 introduces LLM-generated descriptions, LoRA-adapted FLUX image synthesis, multimodal filtering, and a BLIP-2-based retrieval architecture with dynamic feature alignment, diversity supervision, and masked feature reasoning.

E1.justification: v4 adds training on SynCPR's synthetic person triplets and actual training/evaluation on the general-image CIRR benchmark. ITCPR retains its reported 2,202 queries and 20,510 gallery images. v3's standalone CUHK-PEDES text-to-person evaluation is removed, although CUHK-PEDES remains an image-generation training source.

E2.justification: v4 Table 1 newly evaluates methods including TransReID, SOLIDER, RaSa, RDE, CoVR-BLIP, LinCIR, CaLa, and SPRC, while v3's SEARLE-XL comparisons disappear. Pic2Word remains. CAL cites the same work as v3's Simple-CCReID, but appears in a standalone image-only comparison rather than the earlier text-fusion comparison.

E3.justification: The replacement experiments introduce substantially different settings: v3 specifies 60-epoch Adam training, batch size 128, and 384×128 inputs; v4's FAFA uses 10 epochs, AdamW, batch size 256, and padded 224×224 inputs. Appendix C.1 additionally introduces 50-epoch CIRR training and subset retrieval metrics. ITCPR's reported test composition remains unchanged.

E4.justification: v3's TINet architecture, fusion, pseudo-word template, and vocabulary-replacement analyses are removed. v4 adds FAFA component ablations, soft-label and feature-selection sensitivity, synthesis filtering and dataset-scale experiments, LoRA-style comparisons, and loss-weight and masking-ratio analyses in Table 2, Figure 5, and Appendix C.

E5.justification: Neither version specifies repeated-run counts or experimental seeds, or reports confidence intervals, run-to-run variability, or significance tests. Both present retrieval point estimates and sensitivity plots without uncertainty estimates.

E6.justification: The Word4Per result series is largely replaced: v3 Table IV includes 47.502 Rank-1 and 56.944 mAP, whereas v4 Table 1 newly reports FAFA at 46.54 and 55.60. These involve different models and training conditions, not a same-setting performance change. v4 also adds CIRR results, including 54.48 Rank-1 in Table S3. Retained Pic2Word scores differ only by rounding.

T1.justification: Although KL-based distribution matching remains an ingredient, v4 introduces substantive mathematical definitions for top-k feature similarity, identity/group-based soft targets, feature-diversity penalties, and bidirectional masked reconstruction in Equations 3–6. These replace v3's TINet-specific mathematical formulation. Neither version presents formal theorems or proofs.

C1.justification: The central contribution shifts from zero-shot retrieval without CPR training triplets using Word4Per to automatic million-scale triplet synthesis and supervised FAFA retrieval. The abstract, introduction, and conclusion now emphasize SynCPR and fine-grained alignment. The underlying CPR task and ITCPR benchmark contributions are retained.

C2.justification: v3's explanations of pseudo-word semantics, background sensitivity, and TINet fusion tradeoffs disappear. v4 develops new interpretations concerning identity consistency in joint image generation, synthetic-image realism, semantic versus identity constraints in soft labels, and feature diversity. Appendix C.4 also identifies excessive masking as a source of training instability.

D1.justification: v4 adds detailed generation prompts, filtering instructions, LoRA settings, image-cropping procedures, H800 hardware information, and FAFA implementation settings in Appendices A and C.1. v3's TINet implementation and timing details are removed. The promised code/data destination changes from Word4Per to Composed_Person_Retrieval; both disclosures remain future-tense.

R1.justification: v4 adds a substantial diffusion-model research strand, including FLUX, LoRA, diffusion transformers, and flow matching, alongside expanded multimodal and composed-retrieval literature. Positioning shifts from an efficient textual-inversion alternative to a synthetic-data and fine-grained alignment contribution. This goes well beyond reference renumbering or publication-metadata updates.

P1.justification: The title, abstract, introduction, method, experiments, and conclusion are extensively rewritten. The seven-section Word4Per narrative becomes five main sections with Appendices A–C. Detailed ITCPR construction moves from Section IV to Appendix B.1, while the dedicated pseudo-word discussion is removed.

P2.justification: The document changes from a two-column layout to a single-column format, with substantially redesigned architecture diagrams, comparison tables, synthesis examples, and ablation displays. Retained ITCPR annotation and false-negative screening diagrams move from v3 Figures 4–5 to v4 Figures S8–S9. Retrieval visualizations are redrawn for the new method set.

improvement.justification: SynCPR validation across multiple retrievers, FAFA component controls, CIRR evaluation, and detailed synthesis instructions add substantive value. However, v4 omits Word4Per and its measured efficiency evidence while making broad superiority claims on the retained ITCPR benchmark. The changed models and training conditions, without a comparison to the prior approach, leave a material gap in assessing the replacement's advantages. These benefits and losses do not establish a reliable net direction in overall paper quality.
